rule2LeakSamples.label: (ii) E2a — 8 marks
rule2LeakSamples.feedback:
You correctly identify all three exposures — transaction, translation, and economic — and distinguish them with precision. The key distinction between transaction and translation is well handled: you explicitly note that the US subsidiary's net assets are an accounting retranslation rather than a cash settlement, whereas the customer receivables represent real contracted cash flows that move when exchange rates move. The further distinction between transaction and economic exposure — contracted individual invoices versus the long-term competitive impact on uncontracted future sales — is also clearly articulated.

Your management discussion is technically sound across all three types. For transaction exposure, you correctly identify forwards, money-market hedges, options, netting, natural hedging and leading/lagging, and you correctly note the trade-offs (options preserve upside but cost a premium; forwards are certain but remove benefit). For translation exposure, you correctly identify the net investment hedge (USD borrowing offset against USD net assets), discuss matching, and make the important point that hedging a purely accounting exposure can generate real cash costs — so selective hedging is appropriate only where volatility threatens covenants, credit ratings or a disposal. For economic exposure, you correctly conclude that short-term derivatives cannot address it and that the solution lies in operational responses: sourcing in USD, market diversification, pricing flexibility, and production flexibility.

The overall recommendation at the end ties the three together appropriately, noting that each requires a different policy and that the exposures, while overlapping, are not interchangeable. No material omissions or errors.

rule2LeakSamples.label: (i) E3a — 12 marks
rule2LeakSamples.feedback:
You correctly identify that Aldebrino must sell futures, and your contract calculation is right: 48,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 × 6/3 = 96 contracts. The structure of your answer — two scenarios, loan interest plus futures P&L, netting to an effective rate — is also the right framework.

However, you have not applied basis in deriving the expected closing futures price, and this is a material error that flows through every figure.

At the time the hedge is opened, the futures price (95.55) differs from the implied spot price (100 − 4.00 = 96.00). That difference — the basis — is 0.45. Because the futures contract has 9 months of life and the hedge is closed 3 months before expiry (i.e., with 3 months remaining), the unexpired basis at close is 0.45 × 3/9 = 0.15. The expected closing futures price is therefore 100 − new rate − 0.15, not simply 100 − new rate.

For the rate-rise scenario: expected closing price = 100 − 5.00 − 0.15 = 94.85 (you used 95.00). The tick movement is 0.70, not 0.55. The futures gain is 96 contracts × €1m × 0.70% × 3/12 = €168,000, not €132,000. Net six-month cost = €1,320,000 − €168,000 = €1,152,000.

For the rate-fall scenario: expected closing price = 100 − 3.20 − 0.15 = 96.65 (you used 96.80). The tick movement is 1.10, not 1.25. The futures loss is 96 × €1m × 1.10% × 3/12 = €264,000, not €300,000. Net six-month cost = €888,000 + €264,000 = €1,152,000.

The correct effective annual rate in both scenarios is €1,152,000 / (€48m × 6/12) = 4.80%, not 4.95%. Your two scenarios do agree with each other — showing you understand the hedging principle — but they agree at the wrong locked-in rate.

Your alternative derivation (implied futures rate 4.45% + margin 0.50% = 4.95%) also bypasses basis and cannot give the correct answer in a basis-affected hedge.

Your qualitative discussion of basis risk in the limitations section is good, but the concept needed to be applied numerically to derive the closing futures prices.

rule2LeakSamples.label: (i) E3a — 12 marks
rule2LeakSamples.feedback:
You correctly identify that Aldebrino should sell futures, and your contract count of 96 is right (€48m ÷ €1m × 6/3). Your loan interest calculations for both scenarios are also correct: €1.320m at 5.5% and €0.888m at 3.7%.

The material error is that you do not calculate basis and apply it when estimating the closing futures price. Basis at the start of the hedge is (100 − 4.00) − 95.55 = 0.45. Because the futures expire in nine months but Aldebrino closes them in six months (three months before expiry), the unexpired basis is 0.45 × 3/9 = 0.15. The expected closing futures price in each scenario is therefore 100 − prevailing rate − 0.15, not simply 100 − prevailing rate.

Using 100 − rate directly, you arrive at closing prices of 95.00 and 96.80. The correct closing prices are 94.85 (rates rise) and 96.65 (rates fall). This drives the wrong futures profit/loss: you calculate a gain of €132,000 and a loss of €300,000, whereas the correct figures are a gain of €168,000 and a loss of €264,000. Both net six-month costs should be €1,152,000, giving an effective annual rate of 4.80%, not the 4.95% you report.

Your answer does acknowledge basis risk in the limitations section, which is the right concept, but that acknowledgement needs to feed into the actual calculation — the unexpired basis must be deducted from (or added to) the naïve closing futures price to produce the correct locked-in rate.

The structure of your answer is sound: same net cost in both scenarios, correct direction of trade, clear presentation. The single omission of the basis adjustment is what changes the locked-in rate from the correct answer.
